analysis.one_liner: Requires water systems to replace lead service lines, test for lead, hand out filters, and bans lead plumbing.
analysis.headline: The lead-free drinking water bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced water systems that exceed lead limits to replace at least 10% of their lead service lines every year until all are gone, hand out certified water filters to homes, schools, and day cares, and warn customers within 30 days — with warnings printed on water bills. It would have required annual lead testing in schools, banned high-lead plumbing fittings within a year and all non-lead-free plumbing within five, and authorized $200 million a year for replacements, including $40 million a year for the District of Columbia. It never received any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents served by water systems with lead service lines or lead exceedances — above all infants, children, and pregnant women, whom the bill prioritizes for line replacement and filters. Families would get free certified filters, plain-language warnings on their water bills, and their own test results within 14 days. Schoolchildren would gain from required annual testing and remediation in schools. District of Columbia residents, still reeling from the 2004 lead crisis, were singled out for $40 million a year in replacement funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families on lead-tainted water, especially children

how_it_helps.text: Requires water systems to replace at least 10% of their lead service lines every year once lead exceeds the limit, prioritizing homes with high lead levels and buildings serving infants, children, and pregnant women, and forbidding systems from dodging replacement through testing gimmicks.

Requires water systems to provide free certified lead-reduction filters and replacement cartridges to residences, schools, and day care facilities in affected service areas, not just homes known to have lead lines.

Requires much faster and clearer public warnings: notice within 30 days of a lead exceedance and every 90 days after, a lead warning printed on every water bill, and each home's own test results delivered within 14 days — in plain language and in other languages where communities need them.

Requires every state to set up a program of annual lead testing and remediation in schools and educational facilities, with results posted for parents to inspect, and directs the EPA to run the program itself in any state that refuses.

Bans plumbing fittings and fixtures containing more than 2% lead within one year, requires fully lead-free plumbing within five years, and imposes third-party certification and an import cutoff if standards are not tightened.
Authorizes $200 million a year for fiscal 2006–2010 to help pay for lead service line replacement, including $40 million a year specifically for the District of Columbia.

analysis.who_pays: Water utilities and their ratepayers would bear most of the cost: annual replacement of lead lines, free filters for entire affected service areas, biannual monitoring, reoptimized corrosion control, and permanent public education programs. The $200 million-a-year federal authorization is small relative to the nationwide cost of replacing lead service lines, so much of the bill would land on water bills. Plumbing and fixture manufacturers would face a one-year deadline to stop selling high-lead fittings, a five-year lead-free mandate, and third-party certification costs. Federal taxpayers would fund the authorized grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Water utilities, ratepayers, and plumbing makers

drawbacks.text: The mandates are expensive and mostly unfunded: systems must replace 10% of lead lines annually and give filters to every home, school, and day care in an affected area — even homes not known to have lead lines — while the $200 million-a-year authorization is far below the national cost of replacement, so water bills would rise, hitting low-income households too.

The bill itself concedes a technical risk its critics could fairly raise: replacing only part of a lead line can temporarily raise lead levels, so it builds in an exemption process for homeowners who refuse replacement after three attempts.

Tight deadlines — a finished EPA lead rule within 18 months, a plumbing standard overhaul within a year, school regulations within 270 days — could strain the agency and industry, and the lead-free plumbing deadline within five years would raise manufacturing costs passed on to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: lead has no known safe level for children, and the bill directly targets the exposure pathway — lead service lines and fixtures — while prioritizing the most vulnerable. The costs are real and fall on utilities, ratepayers, and manufacturers, and the federal money covers only a fraction of replacement costs. A fair reading is that the bill traded higher water bills and compliance costs for removing a proven neurotoxin from tap water, with the burden landing partly on the same households it protects; the main design weakness is the modest federal funding behind a large unfunded mandate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never held a hearing or markup, so it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim Jeffords, an Independent from Vermont, introduced the bill with Sen. Paul Sarbanes of Maryland on June 29, 2005, in the aftermath of Washington, DC's lead-in-water crisis, which the bill's title and its $40 million-a-year DC funding line addressed directly.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction — its only action of record.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the bill sat in committee until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Water utilities and plumbing manufacturers were better off because the bill died — they avoided the line replacement, filter, and lead-free plumbing mandates. Families served by systems with lead lines gained nothing and kept the status quo risk.

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Lead-Free Drinking Water Act of 2005 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. James Inhofe (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — allowing the bill to die at the end of the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party split is on record; it was sponsored by an Independent with a single Democratic cosponsor and no Republican support listed.

industries.note: Systems exceeding lead limits would have to replace 10% of lead lines annually, hand out free filters, warn customers on every water bill, monitor biannually, and run permanent education programs — costs they would pass largely to ratepayers, with only modest federal grant help. The industry's interest in avoiding these mandates runs against the public's interest in lead-free water.

The bill would ban fittings and fixtures with more than 2% lead within one year, require fully lead-free plumbing within five years, and mandate third-party certification, with an import and commerce cutoff if standards were not revised. Manufacturers' interest in selling cheaper high-lead fittings ran against the public's interest in lead-free plumbing.

Water systems would be required to buy ANSI/NSF-certified lead-reduction filters and replacement cartridges for residences, schools, and day cares in affected areas, creating a guaranteed market. The filters would also directly protect the families receiving them.
